did_you_know.text: The phrase “crimson worm” does not necessarily describe a worm sewn into the garment; it is the name of a deep red dye obtained in antiquity from an animal-based source.
The craftsmen hammered gold into very thin sheets, cut them into threads, and worked them into the fabric. This was a highly delicate textile technique.
The names of the Israelites were engraved on two onyx stones, probably six names on each. In this way, the priests symbolically carried the whole nation on their shoulders.
The breastplate was square and folded double, with each side measuring a zeret—an ancient length roughly equal to the width of a spread hand.
The twelve stones represented the twelve tribes of Israel, with one tribe’s name on each stone. The breastplate thus became a kind of map preserving the nation’s memory.
The breastplate’s chains are described as “a braided work,” meaning they were woven or twisted together. Braided gold jewelry was also known in other ancient cultures.
A blue cord fastened the breastplate to the ephod so that it would not shift. This practical solution kept a complex, heavy garment securely in place while walking.
The robe had a reinforced neck opening so that it would not tear. Modern clothing also often uses reinforcement around openings that receive extra strain.
The bells and pomegranates were hung alternately around the robe’s hem. The bells’ sound marked the priest’s movement as he walked.
The word shesh generally refers to fine linen, a fabric made from flax fibers. Linen was an important and widely used material in the ancient world.
The words “Holy to the LORD” were engraved like the design on an ancient seal, a method meant to leave a clear and lasting mark.
The chapter repeatedly emphasizes that the work was done “as the LORD commanded Moses.” This repetition presents precision and faithfulness as central values in building the Tabernacle.
The Tabernacle consisted of many parts—curtains, boards, bars, pillars, and bases—so it could be dismantled and transported from place to place.
Moses inspected the work before blessing the people. The chapter thus suggests that leadership includes both responsible evaluation and gratitude and encouragement.
